newsitem.title: USA: White House welcomes Republican budget offering.
newsitem.headline: White House welcomes Republican budget offering.

text.p: The White House said on Monday it expected Congress to release its economic assumptions in time for the administration's new budget, calling this a good sign of cooperation from Republicans.

A spokesman for the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which prepares the president's budget, said the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), which tracks the budget for Congress, was expected to send the White House the figures early next week.

President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, has fought bitterly with the Republican-controlled Congress during the past two years over how to balance the budget, including over the arcane issue of whether to use OMB or CBO figures.
After months of political warfare, the White House made a major concession a year ago by deciding to use the congressional numbers instead of its own.

White House officials welcomed the CBO's decision to release the figures earlier than usual. Normally they would not be given out until early next year, too late for the administration's budget proposal, which is due in Feburary.
"We went back and forth, back and forth all last year during the great budget war of 1995 and 1996 on the question of (economic) assumptions," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
"So the fact that both staffs are talking to each other, and trying to get a better expert agreement on what the future of the economy might look like is very encouraging," he said.
"Whether it makes any material difference in drafting a budget proposal remains to be seen at this point."

While also welcoming the CBO's decision, OMB spokesman Larry Haas sounded a cautionary note, saying the economic assumptions would be useful but were not all the information that the administration wanted.

Haas said that included CBO's "technical" assumptions on the government's expected tax revenues as well as its expected spending on the Medicare and Medicaid health care programmes for the poor and elderly.
"Anything we get, any knowledge we have, will obviously inform us," Haas said, but added: "You need the technical assumptions ... (and) that is further down the road."

In another sign that the path to balancing the budget may be growing easier, OMB said that it, and the CBO, are expected to release reduced deficit projections for the year 2002, the target date for a balanced budget.
Haas said that CBO's 2002 deficit forecast was expected to be around $150 billion, while OMB's was likely to be closer to $100 billion. A year ago, CBO had put the 2002 deficit above $200 billion.
Robert Reischauer, a former CBO director who is now a budget expert at the Brookings Institution, played down the importance of the CBO's handing over the figures early.
"It's of modest importance," Reischauer said. "It can be viewed in one sense as helpful to the administration and in another sense as competitive.

"The administration was saying, 'Look, we promised to balance the budget under CBO numbers -- how can we prepare a budget without those assumptions?' Congress is saying, 'Here, we'll give you some of their assumptions so you won't have that excuse.'"
